provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Review of JSS2 Work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall basic concepts of crop production.
The students should be able to list the major branches of horticulture.
The students should be able to explain the importance of agriculture in Nigeria.

Introduction:
Today we will quickly revise what we learned in JSS2 about crop production and horticulture. This will help us build a strong foundation for the new topics we will study this term.

Content:
Crop production is the science and practice of growing crops for food, fiber, and other useful products. In Nigeria, crops like maize, cassava, and yams are very important for food security. Horticulture is a branch of agriculture that deals with the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers, and ornamental plants. Some examples in Nigeria include growing tomatoes, peppers, and flowers like hibiscus. The main branches of agriculture include crop production, livestock farming, forestry, and fisheries. Agriculture is very important in Nigeria as it provides food, creates jobs, earns foreign exchange, and raw materials for industries.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups of four to create a mind map showing the relationship between different branches of agriculture and their importance in Nigeria.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is crop production?
2. List three examples of horticultural crops in Nigeria.
3. Explain why agriculture is important to Nigeria's economy.
4. Differentiate between crop production and horticulture.

Summary:
Today we reviewed the basic concepts of crop production and horticulture that we learned in JSS2, which will help us understand our new topics better.

topics.title: Soil Management
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different methods of erosion control.
The students should be able to explain the concept of crop rotation.
The students should be able to describe the benefits of cover cropping.

Introduction:
We have learned that soil is a vital resource for crop growth. Today we will discuss how to manage soil properly to prevent erosion and maintain fertility, which are important for successful farming in Nigeria.

Content:
Soil erosion is the washing or blowing away of the top fertile soil layer. In Nigeria, during the harmattan season, strong winds can cause soil erosion, while heavy rains during the wet season can wash away soil from farmlands. Erosion control methods include building terraces on slopes, planting grass strips along contours, constructing check dams, and mulching with materials like rice husks or dry grass. Crop rotation is the practice of growing different types of crops in the same area in sequential seasons. For example, planting maize one season, followed by legumes like beans or cowpea the next season. This helps prevent the build-up of pests and diseases and improves soil fertility. Cover cropping involves planting crops that cover the soil surface, such as legumes or grasses, when the main cash crop is not growing. These cover crops protect the soil from erosion, add organic matter when plowed under, and can fix nitrogen from the air into the soil.

Class activity:
Students will visit the school farm (or create a small demonstration plot) to observe and identify different erosion control measures already in place, and suggest additional improvements.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is soil erosion?
2. List three methods of controlling soil erosion in Nigeria.
3. Explain how crop rotation helps maintain soil fertility.
4. Why is cover cropping important during the dry season in northern Nigeria?

Summary:
Proper soil management through erosion control, crop rotation, and cover cropping is essential for maintaining healthy and productive soil for crop growth in Nigeria.

topics.title: Crop Planting Techniques
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate advanced planting methods.
The students should be able to determine proper spacing and depth for different crops.
The students should be able to explain the importance of correct planting techniques.

Introduction:
After discussing soil management, we now focus on how to properly plant crops. The way we plant seeds or seedlings greatly affects their growth and yield, so it's important to learn the right techniques.

Content:
Advanced planting methods include broadcasting, drilling, dibbling, and transplanting. Broadcasting is scattering seeds by hand over a prepared seedbed, commonly used for crops like maize and millet in Nigerian smallholder farms. Drilling involves placing seeds in furrows at specific depths and spacing, often used for crops like sorghum and soybeans. Dibbling is making small holes in the soil and placing a few seeds in each hole, suitable for crops like maize and melons. Transplanting involves growing seedlings in a nursery bed and then moving them to the main field, commonly used for crops like tomatoes, pepper, and cabbage in Nigeria. Spacing refers to the distance between plants within rows and between rows. For example, maize is usually spaced 25-30cm within rows and 75-90cm between rows, while cassava is spaced 1m between plants. Planting depth is how deep seeds are placed in the soil. Generally, small seeds like rice are planted shallow (2-3cm), while larger seeds like maize and beans are planted deeper (4-5cm). The planting depth should be about 3 times the diameter of the seed.

Class activity:
Students will practice different planting methods in the school farm, broadcasting maize seeds, drilling sorghum, dibbling melon seeds, and transplanting tomato seedlings while maintaining proper spacing and depth.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between broadcasting and drilling?
2. Why is proper spacing important for crop growth?
3. How deep should maize seeds be planted and why?
4. Give one crop in Nigeria that is commonly transplanted and explain why this method is used.

Summary:
Using proper planting techniques with correct spacing and depth is crucial for optimal crop growth and yield in Nigerian farming systems.

topics.title: Fertilizer Management
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the process of organic composting.
The students should be able to develop a fertilizer schedule for a common Nigerian crop.
The students should be able to differentiate between organic and inorganic fertilizers.

Introduction:
Just as humans need food to grow healthy, crops need nutrients to thrive. Today we will learn how to provide these nutrients through organic composting and proper fertilizer scheduling.

Content:
Organic composting is the process of decomposing organic materials like crop residues, animal manure, kitchen waste, and other plant materials to create a nutrient-rich soil conditioner. In Nigeria, common materials used for composting include maize stalks, rice husks, cow dung, and poultry droppings. To make compost, these materials are piled in layers, kept moist but not waterlogged, and turned regularly to allow proper decomposition. The process usually takes 2-3 months in the Nigerian climate. Fertilizer scheduling is the planned application of fertilizers at specific times during the growing season to meet crop nutrient needs. For example, for a maize crop in Nigeria, fertilizer might be applied at planting (basal application), 4 weeks after planting (top-dressing), and just before tasseling. The amount and type of fertilizer depend on the soil type, crop requirements, and growth stage. Organic fertilizers like compost and manure release nutrients slowly and improve soil structure, while inorganic fertilizers like NPK provide immediate nutrient availability but can lead to soil degradation if overused.

Class activity:
Students will prepare a small compost heap using materials collected from the school farm and surrounding areas, monitoring its decomposition over the next few weeks.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three materials commonly used for composting in Nigeria.
2. Explain the process of making organic compost.
3. Why is fertilizer scheduling important for crop production?
4. Compare organic and inorganic fertilizers.

Summary:
Proper fertilizer management through organic composting and scheduling is essential for providing crops with the nutrients they need for healthy growth and good yields in Nigerian agriculture.

topics.title: MID-TERM TEST
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate knowledge of topics covered in weeks 1-4.
The students should be able to apply concepts learned to solve agricultural problems.

Introduction:
Today we will have our mid-term test to assess your understanding of the topics we have covered so far this term. This will help me know which areas we need to review more.

Content:
The test will cover the following topics: Review of JSS2 work, Soil Management, Crop Planting Techniques, and Fertilizer Management. You will need to recall definitions, explain concepts, and apply what you have learned to agricultural scenarios. The test will consist of multiple choice questions, short answer questions, and one problem-solving question related to crop production in Nigeria. Make sure to read each question carefully before answering, and manage your time wisely since you have 40 minutes to complete the test.

Class activity:
Students will complete the mid-term test individually, demonstrating their knowledge of the topics covered in the first four weeks of the term.

Evaluation questions:
The mid-term test will serve as the evaluation, with questions covering all topics from weeks 1-4.

Summary:
The mid-term test has assessed your understanding of the fundamental concepts of horticulture and crop production that we have covered so far this term.

topics.title: Crop Irrigation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define irrigation and list different irrigation methods.
The students should be able to explain the importance of irrigation in Nigerian agriculture.
The students should be able to describe basic maintenance of irrigation systems.

Introduction:
After our mid-term break, we are back to learn about crop irrigation. In many parts of Nigeria, rainfall is not sufficient for year-round farming, making irrigation essential for consistent crop production.

Content:
Irrigation is the artificial application of water to land or soil to assist in the growth of agricultural crops. In Nigeria, where rainfall patterns vary greatly between regions and seasons, irrigation is crucial for growing crops during the dry season. Methods of irrigation include surface irrigation (like furrow and basin irrigation), sprinkler irrigation, and drip irrigation. Surface irrigation is commonly used in Nigeria as it's simple and requires less equipment. Water is simply allowed to flow over the field from channels. Sprinkler irrigation uses sprinklers to distribute water like rain, suitable for crops like maize and vegetables. Drip irrigation applies water slowly and directly to the plant roots through small tubes, very efficient but requires more investment. Irrigation is important because it allows farmers to grow crops all year, increases crop yields, ensures food security, and makes it possible to grow high-value crops like tomatoes and onions. Maintenance of irrigation systems involves regular checking for leaks, clearing blockages in pipes and sprinklers, proper storage during off-seasons, and ensuring water sources are clean. In northern Nigeria, traditional irrigation systems like the fadama system have been used for centuries and still play an important role in agriculture today.

Class activity:
Students will design a simple drip irrigation system using plastic bottles to demonstrate how water can be efficiently delivered to plant roots.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is irrigation and why is it important in Nigeria?
2. List three methods of irrigation and explain one.
3. Why is maintenance of irrigation systems necessary?
4. How does irrigation help farmers during the harmattan season in Nigeria?

Summary:
Irrigation is a vital practice in Nigerian agriculture that enables year-round crop production through various methods, each with specific advantages and maintenance requirements.

topics.title: MID-TERM BREAK
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to rest and recharge for the second half of the term.
The students should be able to reflect on what they have learned so far.

Introduction:
This week is our mid-term break, a time to rest and recover from the first half of the term. It's also a good opportunity to reflect on what we have learned about horticulture and crop production.

Content:
During this break, you should take time to rest and relax. You might also want to revisit your notes from the first six weeks to reinforce your understanding of the topics we have covered. Think about how these agricultural practices apply to real-life farming in Nigeria. Observe farming activities in your local community during this period and try to identify the practices we have discussed, such as soil management techniques or irrigation systems. When we return, we will continue with new topics in our scheme of work.

Class activity:
No formal class activity during the break. Students are encouraged to rest and engage in recreational activities.

Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during the break period.

Summary:
Enjoy your mid-term break and return refreshed and ready to continue learning about horticulture and crop production.
